Request.theme: expense fraud with access records and document metadata

Metadata.title: The Vanishing Receipts
Metadata.description: A mid-level finance employee is found dead shortly after flagging suspicious expense reimbursements. The case hinges on access logs and subtle document metadata left behind in routine office systems.
Metadata.briefing: Portland Police respond to a death in a finance office after-hours, days after an internal expense audit started turning up altered receipts. Someone used ordinary office access and everyday file workflows to hide a trail—until a single overlooked metadata artifact ties it together.

Blueprint.crimeMechanism: Jordan Kim entered the company’s downtown office after-hours using a still-active badge that Facilities had temporarily extended for a late client deliverable. He confronted the victim (who had stayed late to reconcile reimbursements), then caused death by manual strangulation in a small copy/records room where there is no camera coverage. He then used an unlocked workstation left in ‘quick lock’ mode and a shared scanner to replace several PDF receipt files in a reimbursement packet with edited versions, relying on routine sync to overwrite prior copies. He concealed the trail by deleting the local ‘Recent files’ list and removing printed audit notes from the victim’s desk, but overlooked document metadata and a forensic artifact linking the edit session to the device used to access the file share.
Blueprint.culpritObjective: Stop the victim from escalating a flagged reimbursement packet and prevent repayment/discipline for a specific inflated travel claim; the incident happened now because the audit was scheduled to be finalized the next morning and the victim had emailed that she would ‘freeze’ reimbursement processing at close of business.
Blueprint.caseHook: The key break comes from ordinary PDF properties: an innocuous ‘Author’ string and a scanner job ID that survives file overwrites, allowing a forensic join between a nameless edit session and a physical device in the office.

incidentSequence.event: Victim sends an internal email stating reimbursement processing will be frozen pending audit reconciliation.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: An internal email from the victim at 4:41 PM mentions putting a hold on reimbursements pending audit reconciliation.

incidentSequence.event: Jordan uses his badge at the 3rd-floor east stairwell reader to enter the finance suite after hours.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: Access control logs show a single entry at 6:57 PM through the 3rd-floor east stairwell into the finance suite.

incidentSequence.event: Jordan confronts the victim in the copy/records room; he strangles her during a brief struggle.
Jordan uses an unlocked workstation to overwrite receipt PDFs in the reimbursement packet folder, relying on sync to propagate the new versions.
Morning staff discover the victim unresponsive in the copy/records room and call 911.
incidentSequence.publicDescription: At 7:22 AM, staff reported finding the victim unresponsive in a small copy/records room within the finance suite.

clueLadder.discovery: A shared folder named "Finance\Reimbursements\Q1\Packet_0312" shows receipt PDFs modified between "2026-03-12 19:26" and "2026-03-12 19:31" in the file server audit view.
clueLadder.inference: The reimbursement packet was actively altered after normal business hours close to the estimated incident window, indicating concealment activity tied to the fraud theme.

clueLadder.discovery: The access control report lists badge ID "BK-44719" assigned to "Jordan Kim" with an entry at "2026-03-12 18:57:12" at "3F East Stairwell Reader."
clueLadder.inference: Jordan had physical access to the finance suite after hours at a time consistent with the opportunity to confront the victim and access office systems.

clueLadder.discovery: The file server audit log shows user "SYNC-SVC" recorded overwrite events with session token "S-9c2f1" for files "Hotel_Receipt.pdf" and "Mileage_Log.pdf" at "2026-03-12 19:28:11" and "19:29:03."
clueLadder.inference: A specific opaque session token carried out the critical overwrite actions, but the actor is not identified by name at this stage.

clueLadder.discovery: The PDF properties for "Hotel_Receipt.pdf" (modified copy) list Author as "J.Kim" and Producer as "Microsoft Print to PDF" with CreationDate "2026-03-12T19:24:58-07:00."
clueLadder.inference: The edited receipt bears a human-entered author string consistent with Jordan’s initials and was produced via a typical office PDF workflow shortly before the overwrite window.

clueLadder.discovery: The IT asset inventory lists workstation "FIN-WS-03" assigned to the finance suite copy/records room, with its wired MAC ending ":7B:19".
clueLadder.inference: A physical workstation in the same room as the victim can be referenced by a stable hardware identifier that can later be matched to network/session artifacts.

clueLadder.discovery: Forensic review of the file server’s security log bundle shows session token "S-9c2f1" authenticated from source IP "10.44.8.23" at "2026-03-12 19:27:49", and DHCP maps "10.44.8.23" to MAC ending ":7B:19" at lease start "2026-03-12 18:50:00".
clueLadder.inference: The overwrite session token can be objectively linked to the copy/records room workstation, placing the actor at that specific device during the concealment actions shortly after the estimated incident time.

redHerrings.suspicion: Facilities could have manipulated badge access to enter after hours and frame someone via access logs.
redHerrings.verification: The access system admin log shows a change ticket "FAC-11802" approved at "2026-03-11 14:06" that extended after-hours access for badge "BK-44719" only; the admin action is recorded under username "chart" at "2026-03-11 14:09:33".
redHerrings.resolution: The logged change is a narrow, pre-scheduled permission extension tied to Jordan’s badge and does not provide Colin with after-hours entry under his own badge for the relevant door/time.

redHerrings.suspicion: Accounts payable had direct access to reimbursement files and could have altered PDFs to hide mistakes or fraud.
redHerrings.verification: VPN logs list Maya Reed’s account "mreed" connected from public IP "73.19.204.55" from "2026-03-12 18:10" to "18:46", while the file server overwrite events for the packet occur at "19:28:11" and "19:29:03".
redHerrings.resolution: The verified remote connection window ends before the overwrite timestamps, weakening the theory that Maya performed the after-hours overwrite actions at the critical time.

redHerrings.suspicion: Finance leadership might have wanted the audit stopped and could pressure staff or cover up by altering packet documents.
redHerrings.verification: Building lobby visitor log shows Elena Soto signed out at "2026-03-12 17:52" and the parking garage exit reader logs her vehicle tag "OR 684-KQJ" at "2026-03-12 17:59:14".
redHerrings.resolution: These records support that Elena left the premises before the after-hours entry and overwrite window, making direct on-site involvement less consistent with the timeline.

SuspectFull.name: Jordan Kim
SuspectFull.relationship: Frequent reimbursement claimant whose expense packet was being reviewed by the victim
SuspectFull.motive: Jordan had a specific travel reimbursement packet under scrutiny, and a pending dispute risked forcing him to repay an inflated claim and triggering an HR or compliance review. The victim’s end-of-day message about freezing reimbursements created a narrow window where his claim could be challenged or halted before it was finalized the next morning.
SuspectFull.alibi: Jordan says he was at the downtown office after hours to finish a late client deliverable under a temporary Facilities access extension; building access logs can confirm an entry through the 3rd-floor east stairwell at 6:57 PM. He has no independent witness continuously with him inside the finance suite, and the copy/records room area has limited camera coverage.
SuspectFull.background:
Jordan Kim is a project manager known for frequent work travel and routine expense reimbursements.

His badge permissions were temporarily extended by Facilities for late-hours access tied to a deliverable.

He had an active reimbursement dispute in the same period the victim was reconciling and preparing to freeze processing.

Jordan had practical familiarity with the company’s office workflows, including shared folders and scanning/printing receipts for reimbursement packets.

SuspectFull.name: Colin Hart
SuspectFull.relationship: Building access administrator for the victim’s office suite
SuspectFull.motive: The victim’s reimbursement freeze threatened to trigger an audit that would draw attention to how after-hours access exceptions were being requested and approved. Colin also had an incentive to avoid scrutiny or complaints about his access-control change handling if the dispute escalated to leadership.
SuspectFull.alibi: He states he was off-site and working through routine access requests from home the evening of 2026-03-12; his home internet activity and device login history can be checked against his account usage. The limitation is that some of his Facilities work involves remote administrative actions that don’t require him to be physically present in the building.
SuspectFull.background: Colin Hart is a contracted facilities/security administrator responsible for scheduling and approving badge access changes for the downtown office. Building systems record his username on access-change tickets, including narrowly scoped extensions for individual badges. His role gives him administrative visibility into access reports and the ability to process after-hours access exceptions through documented change requests.

SuspectFull.name: Elena Soto
SuspectFull.relationship: Victim’s department head overseeing the audit and performance
SuspectFull.motive: The reimbursement freeze threatened to derail a high-visibility audit closeout and expose control gaps on Elena’s watch. She had a personal stake in keeping the finance team’s metrics and leadership credibility intact ahead of reporting deadlines.
SuspectFull.alibi: Building records show she signed out in the lobby at 17:52 and a parking garage exit reader logged her vehicle tag (OR 684-KQJ) at 17:59:14, both before the after-hours activity window. The verification depends on badge/vehicle systems and assumes she did not return using alternative transportation later that evening.
SuspectFull.background: Elena Soto is the finance director responsible for oversight of reimbursement controls and the victim’s team performance. She had direct professional visibility into the flagged packet and the internal email about freezing reimbursements pending audit reconciliation. She works primarily on-site during business hours and is documented leaving the premises before the evening window when the reimbursement packet was altered.

SuspectFull.name: Maya Reed
SuspectFull.relationship: Worked closely with the victim on reimbursements and the Q1 packet workflow
SuspectFull.motive: The victim’s decision to freeze reimbursements threatened to expose errors or irregularities in a packet Maya helped assemble and would likely trigger scrutiny of her processing and sign-offs. She also had reason to want a flagged packet corrected quickly to avoid a public escalation to audit leadership and the resulting reputational hit inside the team.
SuspectFull.alibi: Maya reports she was working remotely and connected to the company network via VPN from 6:10 PM to 6:46 PM; VPN authentication logs for account "mreed" corroborate that connection window and source public IP. The VPN records confirm timing and remote access but don’t show what she was doing off-network after disconnecting.
SuspectFull.background:
Maya Reed is an accounts payable specialist with routine access to reimbursement documentation and shared packet folders used by finance.
She regularly coordinated with the victim on receipt completeness, naming conventions, and submission deadlines for reimbursement packets.
Her work is largely administrative but involves handling scanned receipts and PDFs that later feed into audit reconciliation.

AssetFull.title: Witness Statement: Morning Discovery in Copy/Records Room
AssetFull.description: Sworn statement from a finance staff member describing the 2026-03-13 morning discovery in the copy/records room, including immediate scene observations and what was seen on the FIN-WS-03 workstation. Notes include the shared reimbursement folder path and a visible modified-time window for Packet_0312 receipt PDFs (19:26–19:31 on 2026-03-12).

bodyDoc.title: WITNESS STATEMENT
bodyDoc.subtitle: Morning Discovery in Copy/Records Room (Finance Suite) — Portland, Oregon

sections.heading: STATEMENT OF
sections.text:
I am an employee in the finance department in the downtown office in Portland. I am giving this statement about what I saw the morning the victim was found in the copy/records room.

I understand this statement may be used in a criminal investigation. I swear/affirm the information I provide is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

sections.heading: Oath / Advisement
sections.text: I was advised that giving false information is a crime. I am providing this statement voluntarily.

sections.heading: Narrative
sections.text:
On 2026-03-13, I arrived to work in the morning and went into the finance suite. I walked toward the copy/records room area.

When I opened the copy/records room, I saw the victim on the floor and she was not responding. I backed out and notified others and 911 was called. I did not move anything in the room.

Before police arrived, I noticed the workstation in the copy/records room was on. I did not sit down and work, but I looked at the monitor from where I was standing. A file window was open to a shared folder path that I recognized as:

- `Finance\Reimbursements\Q1\Packet_0312`

In that folder view, I could see receipt PDFs listed, and I could see the “Date modified” column. I remember the modified times were clustered late the prior evening. The times I saw on the screen were between approximately 19:26 and 19:31 on 2026-03-12 for multiple receipt PDFs in that Packet_0312 folder.

I did not click into any files, print anything, or change anything. After noticing the folder listing, I left the area and waited for instructions.

items.label: Modified-time window observed in folder listing
items.value: Between 2026-03-12 19:26 and 2026-03-12 19:31 (as shown in the “Date modified” column)

items.label: Interaction with workstation/files
items.value: Witness states they only looked at the screen; did not click/open/print/modify anything.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Witness describes what was visible on the workstation screen at the time of discovery and recalls the folder path and a modified-time range. The statement does not, by itself, identify who made the modifications or which specific PDFs were changed.

sections.heading: Documented observations
sections.text: - A shared folder named "Finance\Reimbursements\Q1\Packet_0312" shows receipt PDFs modified between "2026-03-12 19:26" and "2026-03-12 19:31" in the file server audit view.

ResultAssets.title: Forensic Timeline Correlation Report: Session Token to Endpoint (S-9c2f1 → 10.44.8.23 / :7B:19)
ResultAssets.description: Time-aligned correlation report linking file-server session token S-9c2f1 to source IP 10.44.8.23 and a DHCP lease mapping that IP to MAC suffix :7B:19 during the 2026-03-12 after-hours overwrite window. Includes key timestamps from the submitted VPN/file-share extract and limitations regarding clock drift and identity attribution.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: A timeline correlation was performed using the bounded, time-stamped entries contained in the submitted log extract (document.vpn_log_extract_mreed_20260312). Relevant events were listed and compared by timestamp to identify temporal relationships between (a) session-token authentication metadata (token, source IP, DHCP lease mapping) and (b) the after-hours file-share activity window present in the same extract. All times are reported as recorded in the provided records and anchored to the case incident date (2026-03-12) and case opened time (2026-03-13T09:05:00-07:00).

sections.heading: Findings
sections.text: The submitted extract contains a time window showing after-hours modification activity in the folder "Finance\\Reimbursements\\Q1\\Packet_0312" (19:26–19:31 on 2026-03-12) and identifies overwrite events attributed to service user "SYNC-SVC" with session token "S-9c2f1". The canonical security/DHCP correlation associated with this session token indicates the token "S-9c2f1" authenticated from source IP "10.44.8.23" at "2026-03-12 19:27:49" and that DHCP maps "10.44.8.23" to a MAC ending ":7B:19" with lease start "2026-03-12 18:50:00".

ResultEmails.subject: DFU Report (Timeline Correlation): S-9c2f1 session token → 10.44.8.23 / :7B:19 (case_graph_detective_205)
ResultEmails.body:
Detective Leland,

Per request, we completed a **timeline correlation** on the submitted log extract (**document.vpn_log_extract_mreed_20260312**, from **asset.gps_track**) and aligned the key after-hours activity entries to the correlated session authentication/DHCP mapping associated with the overwrite session token.

In the submitted file-share audit view, the folder **Finance\\Reimbursements\\Q1\\Packet_0312** shows a modification burst window between **2026-03-12 19:26** and **19:31**. Within that window, the audit log records two overwrite events by service user **SYNC-SVC** with session token **S-9c2f1**: **Hotel_Receipt.pdf** at **2026-03-12 19:28:11** and **Mileage_Log.pdf** at **2026-03-12 19:29:03**.

The correlated security/DHCP data for this analysis associates **session token S-9c2f1** with an authentication from **source IP 10.44.8.23** at **2026-03-12 19:27:49**, and shows DHCP mapping **10.44.8.23** to a MAC ending **:7B:19** with lease start **2026-03-12 18:50:00**. This supports linkage of the overwrite session activity to a specific internal endpoint identity (IP→MAC) during the relevant timeframe.

Please note the stated limitations: **independent clock sources may drift or use different time zones**, and **temporal correlation does not by itself establish identity**. The attached report documents the correlated timestamps and identifiers as observed.

Briefing.subject: Assignment: The Vanishing Receipts — Homicide / Workplace Fraud (case_graph_detective_205)
Briefing.body:
Det. Leland — We’re investigating the death of a mid-level finance employee discovered unresponsive in the finance suite copy/records room the morning after she indicated reimbursements would be frozen pending audit reconciliation. The case presents as Homicide / Workplace Fraud with potential post-incident document manipulation in routine office systems.

What we can currently place with records: after-hours badge entry into the finance suite consistent with the relevant window, and file server audit activity showing overwrites within a shared reimbursement packet folder (including receipt PDFs) shortly after business hours. The modified receipt printout retains PDF properties (Author string, Producer, and creation date) that may indicate who generated the altered version.

What remains uncertain: exact movements inside the suite, the victim’s last confirmed interactions, and whether the overwrite activity reflects deliberate concealment, opportunistic cleanup, or an automated/authorized workflow executed at an unusual time. We also need to clarify how access extensions were requested/approved and whether any account use could reflect credential sharing or a staged trail.

Why this matters now: the apparent convergence of a reimbursement “freeze” message, after-hours access, and near-immediate changes to Packet_0312 creates a narrow, time-sensitive opportunity to preserve and interpret volatile logs and office system artifacts before routine retention and sync cycles degrade them.

Immediate objective: lock down and reconcile access-control entries, file server audit events, and the workstation attribution indicators tied to the copy/records room device, then use that timeline to prioritize interviews (facilities/admin, finance leadership, AP) and determine who had the opportunity and means to be in the room and alter the packet during the critical window.

FollowUpEmails.body:
Det. Leland,

I’m the first PPB patrol supervisor who arrived after the 07:22 call on 2026-03-13. The copy/records room within the finance suite was treated as a restricted area on arrival; staff were told to stay out and not touch the workstation labeled FIN-WS-03, the printer/scanner, or any papers in the room.

Facilities was instructed not to power down or move any equipment from that room pending detectives’ review. The door to the finance suite was controlled while we waited for detectives.

—Sgt. Lena Park
Portland Police Bureau (PPB)

FollowUpEmails.subject: What I saw on FIN-WS-03 during the 07:22 discovery
FollowUpEmails.body:
Detective,

I’m the finance staff member who found her at about 07:22 on 2026-03-13 in the copy/records room.

Before we realized it was an emergency, I glanced at the workstation screen (the one labeled FIN-WS-03). A File Explorer window was already open to the shared folder path “Finance\Reimbursements\Q1\Packet_0312.” I also remember seeing file modified times for receipts clustered around 19:26–19:31 on 2026-03-12.

After I saw her, I backed out and called 911; I didn’t touch the keyboard or mouse.

Alicia Nguyen

QuestionTopics.topic: What exact time did the badge log show entry into the finance suite for badge BK-44719?
During what time window were Packet_0312 receipt PDFs modified, and which two files are explicitly logged as overwritten in that burst?
Which internal endpoint (source IP and MAC suffix) is correlated to the overwrite session token S-9c2f1 during the critical window?

Questions.prompt: What time did badge BK-44719 enter the finance suite, per badge logs?
When were Packet_0312 receipt PDFs modified, and which two files were overwritten in that burst?
During the overwrite window, which internal endpoint (source IP and MAC suffix) correlates to session token S-9c2f1?

Explanation: After the victim froze reimbursements pending audit reconciliation, Jordan Kim used badge BK-44719 to enter the finance suite after hours, confronted her in the copy/records room, and killed her, then immediately tried to erase the fraud trail by overwriting Packet_0312 receipt PDFs via the background sync account. The badge-entry log independently places Jordan in the building at 18:57, matching the narrow window before the edits and the estimated incident time. The decisive link comes from the overwrite session token (S-9c2f1): forensic timeline correlation ties it to IP 10.44.8.23, which DHCP maps to the FIN-WS-03 workstation’s MAC suffix (:7B:19) located in that same copy/records room. The modified Hotel_Receipt.pdf also carries the human-entered Author string “J.Kim” and a creation time minutes before the overwrites, reinforcing that Jordan produced the altered document. The forensic result can’t prove who was physically at the keyboard (clocks can drift and correlation isn’t identity), but combined with Jordan’s unique after-hours access and the document metadata, it triangulates him as the actor behind both the concealment and the killing. The strongest red herrings collapse under time-and-access checks: Maya Reed’s VPN session ends before the overwrite timestamps, Elena Soto is logged leaving before the after-hours window, and Colin Hart’s admin ticket merely extended Jordan’s badge rather than giving Colin a path to be on scene.
